dataset.name: Patch-level CO2 and CH4 fluxes and porewater concentrations in experimental wetlands, 2 PPT saltwater intrusion simulations, Aug-Oct 2022: Louisiana
description: This dataset contains carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) flux measurements from patches of wetland vegetation dominated by Typha domingensis and Panicum hemitomon, which were conducted to assess flux responses to acute saltwater intrusion. The measurements occurred before, during, and after simulated acute saltwater intrusion events of low concentrations of ~ 2 PPT. The measurements comprise gas fluxes from the wetland surface (i.e., soil-water column and vegetation) and fluxes from the soil-water column exclusively. These two sets of fluxes are separated into two files and are complemented with four more files containing porewater concentrations of CO2 and CH4 collected at 0-5 cm, 10-15 cm, and 20-25 cm depth increments, spectral indices measurements, biomass, and sediment elevation table measurements. The files can be opened with regular text editors or spreadsheet programs.

spatialCoverage.description: The University of Louisiana at Lafayette’s Cade Farm is located in St. Martinville Parish, Louisiana. The experimentation took place in the Visser wetland experimental complex composed of eight constructed ecosystem-scale wetland units (50 x 20 m) used for ecological research in fresh and brackish water conditions. Four of the eight wetlands that are used for research in brackish conditions were constructed with underlying industrial-grade High- Density Polyethylene (HDPE) plastic liners that prevent potential pollution of the underlying Chicot aquifer system with the salt water used for experimentation. In 2013, after construction, native vegetation species characteristic of freshwater and brackish wetlands in Louisiana were transplanted from the Rockefeller Refuge and the White Lake Preserves. The plants included the two common upper estuary plants that are featured in this study, Typha domingensis and Panicum hemitomon.

measurementTechnique:
Saltwater intrusion (SWI) events of ~2 PSU salinity and durations of two, six, and nine days were recreated in different wetlands, with a fourth wetland set as a reference (control treatment) with no salinity manipulation. Salinity in this reference wetland remained lower than 0.3 PSU throughout the study but had similar water level fluctuations to the treatments.
Freshwater was pumped into the wetland to raise the water level (30 – 50 cm) while adding a saline brine created with Instant Ocean™ until reaching ~ 2 PSU salt concentrations in the sampling plots (see Step 2). Saline water was pumped out to end the SWI event while freshwater from groundwater wells was pumped in until the salinity returned to freshwater conditions (i.e., < 0.3 PSU) and the water level dropped to previous levels.

For each treatment and the control wetland, carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) fluxes were measured before (up to 43 days), during, and after (up to 5 days) the recreated SWI events. The sampling was conducted in replicated 3 m × 5 m rectangular plots (15 m2) in two distinct patches of vegetation. Within each wetland, two plots were located in patches dominated by Typha and two more in patches dominated by Panicum. We installed two 30.5 × 30.5 (9.3 × 10-2 m^2 surface area of measurement) 10 cm tall, custom-made PVC gas sampling collars within each Typha plot. To conduct the measurements, one transparent top with the same areal dimensions as the collars and 1.52 m tall (14.2 x 10^-2 m^3) was set to create a seal with water in the collar rims, forming a closed chamber. In the Panicum patches, we used a floating version of the transparent tops with the exact areal dimensions as the collars and 61 cm tall (i.e., 5.7 x 10^-2 m^3) in duplicate marked sites to ensure sampling was always on the same spot. The tops were equipped with two 5V fans and a thermometer. These chambers simultaneously recorded gas exchange across the soil-water column and vegetation (i.e., wetland surface). We also deployed a smaller (4.7 x 10-2 m3) translucid chamber inside each collar that did not include vegetation surfaces and recorded only exchange across the soil-water column (i.e., soil-water column). The chambers were connected to a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (Picarro G4301) that recirculated air at a rate of 1 L min^-1 and recorded CO2 and CH4 concentrations at ~1 Hz frequency. The measurements occurred at least 24 hours before or after any salinity concentration increase (start of SWI event) or decrease (end of SWI event).

Before flux calculations, each chamber data was plotted to identify potential sealing failures and trim the data to remove the artificial noise in the signal they created. Flux calculation followed procedures described in Bohrer et al. (2019) and Villa et al. (2021). We fitted a non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981) to the 2-minute CO2 concentrations time series corresponding to each chamber deployment. For CH4, we first plotted the concentration versus time in the 2-minute chamber deployments. We then visually identified chamber runs that had a monotonous increase without rapid concentration increase typically associated with bubbling events. Out of the 179 chamber deployments analyzed, 11 were identified to show such a type of signal. We then calculated the maximum time-step concentration change of all identified chambers. We set this value as an empirical threshold above which any concentration change was deemed to have come from ebullition. The data around the bubbling event was isolated and integrated to calculate the concentration change over time and normalized by the dimensions of the chamber (adjusted for water level), its temperature, and atmospheric pressure during sampling. The data portions not affected by ebullition were readjusted to the concentrations pre-ebullition and then fitted to the same non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model used to determine the CO2 fluxes. The total methane flux in each chamber was calculated by adding the ebullitive and diffusive fluxes, which accounted for the net gas exchange at the wetland surface, soil and water columns, and vegetation inside the chamber.

Porewater at each patch plot was collected using semipermanent “sippers” with a 5-cm depth infiltration surface deployed at 5, 10, and 20 cm depth. Sippers were manufactured from a 2.5 cm diameter White Acetal Resin tube and were sealed with clear cast epoxy and 1 mm thick caps made from the same material. At the top, we attached a 1.57 mm tube connector to 6.35 mm diameter PFA Plastic tubing for water extraction. Samples were collected with 30 mL syringes, stored in 10 mL crimped vials preserved with 0.2 HCL 2M, and refrigerated until processing in the lab.

We used the headspace equilibration technique described by Kampbell et al. (1989) on 25 mL syringes with 5 mL of water from the vial collected in the field and 15 mL of nitrogen gas (N2). The syringes were shaken for 5 minutes using a rocking shaker. We injected 13 mL headspace in 10 mL pre-evacuated sealed glass vials for gas concentration analysis.
CO2 and CH4 concentrations in gaseous form were measured from 0.5-mL headspace subsamples injected in a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (LI-7810, LI-COR) set on a closed loop (e.g., Wilkinson et al., 2018; Villa et al., 2024). Samples were injected using an injection kit (LI-78000-110). The gas concentration in the headspace was calculated from the change in the instrument’s signal after the injection and transformed into the aqueous equivalent concentration using dilution equations.

After conducting gas flux measurements, leaf light absorbance and reflectance were measured using a CI-710 miniature handheld leaf spectrometer (CI-710S, CID Bio-science) to determine spectral indices proxies of plant health and appearance (i.e., NDVI, PSI, PSRI). This device was used on vegetation within the sampling collar (5 leaves) and surrounding vegetation within the sampling plots (5 leaves). The handheld leaf spectrometer device was placed upon the top third of T. domingensis leaves and within the top three leaves of P. hemitomon stems to obtain spectral measurements.

Water levels at central points of each wetland was measured using pressure transducers (CS451, Campbell Scientific). Salinity at each wetland vegetation plots was measured manually during sampling using a multiparameter handheld YSI Model 85 (Oxygen, Conductivity, Salinity, and Temperature) before, during, and after each SWI event. Porewater salinity was measured from the porewater vials using a multifunctional meter (AG51PRO, AERO-GRO) digital multifunctional meter.

Each wetland’ patch had surface elevation tables (SET). The surface elevation change was calculated from two SET measurements conducted twice on 2/25/2022 and 2/25/2023, following procedures described by Boumans & Day (1993) and Cahoon et al. (2002).
Photosynthetic available radiation (PAR) and Solar radiation were recorded with a LI-190R Quantum sensor (LI-190R, LI-COR).
The aboveground biomass within each sampled collar (or matching area below floating chambers) was determined by harvesting (10/11/2022), drying, and weighing.
